title.en: The Succession at the Hall of Banu Sa'idah

region.en: Medina, hall of Banu Sa'idah (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 麥地那薩伊達亭堂（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Event 632 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate: Its Rise, Decline and Fall (1891), ch. 1

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate: Its Rise, Decline and Fall (Religious Tract Society, 1891), ch. 1

texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The Prophet dies; the Ansar gather in the hall of Banu Sa'idah to choose a chief of their own. Abu Bakr and Umar come to them; Abu Bakr reminds them that the Arabs will not accept a chief outside Quraysh — 'the Arabs will not submit but to this tribe of Quraysh.' He takes the hand of Umar and of Abu Ubayda; the Ansar seize Abu Bakr's hand, and the homage is paid. In the hall of Aisha the party of Ali stands apart; but Abu Bakr's election carries, and the first caliph sends the army of Usama within days.
summary.zh: 先知歿；輔士聚於薩伊達亭堂欲自選首領。阿布·伯克爾與歐瑪爾往之；阿布·伯克爾言阿拉伯人必不認古萊氏之外者為主。他舉起歐瑪爾與阿布·烏拜達之手；輔士握阿布·伯克爾之手，效忠遂定。阿伊莎居室一方阿里派另立；然阿布·伯克爾之選成為公論，首任哈里發數日內即遣烏薩瑪之軍。

sensitivity.note: Historiographical tradition (Tabari, Ibn Ishaq) retold in Muir's 1891 narrative; the succession dispute remains a point of Sunni-Shi'i difference; presented as received narrative.

passages.text: While Abu Bakr and Umar were with the Prophet's family in Aisha's chamber, the Ansar gathered in the hall of Banu Sa'idah to choose a chief from among themselves. Abu Bakr and Umar went out to them. Sa'd ibn Ubada was sitting there, and Sad said: 'O company of the Ansar, you have precedence in religion and merit; there is no tribe like you in Islam; so let this matter be among you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Abu Bakr answered: 'Noble as you are, the Arabs will acknowledge authority only in this tribe of Quraysh, who are the core of the Arab race.' Then he took Umar by the hand, and Abu Ubayda; and he said, 'Choose which of these two you will.' But the Ansar said: 'We will not have any but thee, Abu Bakr — thou wast the companion in the cave, the second of the two when they were in the cave.' They seized his hand, and the homage was paid; and the same day the army of Usama was sent forward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: Yarmuk: The Day of Lost Eyes

region.en: Yarmuk river gorge, southern Syria (literal pin)
region.zh: 敘利亞南部雅爾穆克河谷（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 636 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; S. Ockley, History of the Saracens (1890)

source.work: William Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890)

texts.license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The Byzantine host of Heraclius' generals, five times the number of the Muslims, is drawn up at the Yarmuk. Khalid, fresh from the Iraq road, takes the command; the battle sways for days. The women of the Muslim camp fight in the last stand — 'the day of lost eyes', the day when so many lost their sight from the strain; the Byzantine line breaks, and the gorge is choked with fugitives. Syria is won.
summary.zh: 希拉克略諸將之拜占庭大軍，五倍於穆斯林，列陣雅爾穆克。自伊拉克戰場而來的哈立德受命；戰事連日拉鋸。營中婦女參與最後的防線——是日眾多戰士因力竭而失明，故名『失明之日』。拜占庭戰線崩潰，峽谷塞滿敗兵。敘利亞底定。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; battle narrative as received in Muir/Ockley from Tabari.

passages.text: Heraclius had gathered the forces of Byzantium at the Yarmuk — it was said eighty thousand or more — against the Muslim army of less than half the number, under Abu Ubayda, with Khalid ibn al-Walid as the fighting arm. The battle opened in the summer heat; for days the lines swayed back and forth along the gorge of the river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the last stand the Muslim women came out to fight, and the warriors lost their sight from the heat and the strain — so the day was called 'the day of lost eyes.' The Byzantine line broke at last; the horsemen of the empire were driven back on the gorge, and the passage was choked with fugitives. Heraclius, at Antioch, heard the news and left Syria for Constantinople, saying: 'Peace be with thee, O Syria.' And the cities of the coast opened their gates one after another.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 9; not verbatim.

title.en: Qadisiyya: Rustam's Armor and the Three Days
title.zh: 卡迪西亞：魯斯塔姆的鎧甲與三日之戰

region.zh: 伊拉克希拉附近的卡迪西亞（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 637 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 13
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Rustam, the Sasanian commander, arrays the hosts of Persia at Qadisiyya, himself in cuirass and double mail with two coats of gold. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, sick, directs the battle from a castle. For three days and nights the lines fight; on the third night — the Night of Clangour — the Muslims carry the field; a gust of wind covers Rustam with dust, and he is struck down under his baggage-camel. The road to Ctesiphon is open.
summary.zh: 薩珊統帥魯斯塔姆於卡迪西亞列波斯大軍，身披胸甲與雙層鎖子甲，飾以金。賽爾德·本·阿比·瓦卡斯抱病於堡壘中指揮。三日三夜激戰；第三夜——『鏗鏘之夜』——穆斯林取勝；一陣風沙掩覆魯斯塔姆，他於其馱貨駱駝下被擊斃。通往泰西封之路開。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; narrative as received in Muir from Tabari.

passages.text: Rustam, the general of the Sasanian king, brought up the hosts of Persia to the plain of Qadisiyya, himself in a cuirass of gold, with two coats of mail, and a helmet; a herald cried before him. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, sick of the quinsy, directed the battle from the castle of the neighbouring monastery, watching from its towers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 13; not verbatim.

passages.text: For three days and nights the two armies fought in relays; the third was the Night of Clangour, when neither host slept. In the last hour a storm of dust rose against the Persian lines, and Rustam hid himself under the baggage of his camel; a Muslim found him there and struck off his hand, and killed him. The army of Persia broke and fled; the elephant-guard died with their beasts; and the road to Ctesiphon, the royal city, lay open before the Arabs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 13; not verbatim.

region.en: Ctesiphon / Madain, Sasanian capital on the Tigris (literal pin)
region.zh: 底格里斯河畔薩珊都城泰西封（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 637 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 14
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The capital of the Sasanians falls after the siege of the canal line. The Great Hall of Khosrau is entered: the white elephant of the throne, the crown set with jewels, the carpet of the winter palace woven in one piece with its gardens of pearls — the fifth of the spoil set aside, the rest divided. Yazdegerd flees east, and the fire-temples of the Persian heartland are brought under tribute.
summary.zh: 圍攻運河防線後，薩珊都城陷落。庫斯老的偉大宮殿被入：寶座之白象、鑲寶之冠、冬宮以珍珠織成花園的整幅地毯——戰利品的五分之一歸庫，其餘分配。伊嗣俟東逃；波斯腹地的火廟納貢。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the sack of the capital recorded as received narrative.

passages.text: After the victory of Qadisiyya the Arabs crossed the canal line in the storm, and the city of Madain — Ctesiphon, the capital of the Sasanians — was taken. The Great Hall of Khosrau was entered, and the treasure of the crown: the carpet of the winter palace was carried out whole, woven in a single piece with its gardens of gold and silver and pearls, and it was cut into shares by order of Umar, who said that such a thing should not be in one man's keeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 14; not verbatim.

passages.text: Yazdegerd fled eastward from city to city; the fire-temples of the Persian heartland were brought under tribute, and the Arabs recited at the palace: 'How often have they left their gardens and their fountains, their treasures and their splendid dwellings — so it was: and We gave them to the children of Israel for an inheritance.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 14; not verbatim.

title.en: Umar Enters Jerusalem in His Patched Cloak
title.zh: 歐瑪爾披補丁斗篷入耶路撒冷

region.zh: 耶路撒冷阿克薩聖所（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 637-638 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 10
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The patriarch Sophronius surrenders the city on condition that the caliph come in person. Umar rides from Medina with a single camel-servant, the two riding turn about. He enters in a patched mantle, walking; the patriarch reads in his rags the abomination of desolation of Daniel. Terms are granted: the churches safe, the tributary tax; the caliph prays at the sanctuary of David, and the Aqsa is cleared of the city's refuse.
summary.zh: 主教索福羅尼烏斯以哈里發親臨為條件交城。歐瑪爾攜一名駱駝侍者自麥地那啟程，二人輪流騎乘。他徒步披補丁斗篷入城；主教於其襤褸中讀出但以理書之荒涼可憎之物。條款寬厚：教堂得保、納稅而存；哈里發於大衛聖所禮拜，並清出阿克薩的城中穢物。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the Umar tradition underlies the later Covenant of Umar and Muslim-Jewish-Christian relations in the city.

passages.text: The patriarch Sophronius would surrender Jerusalem only to the caliph himself. Umar set out from Medina with one servant and a camel, which they rode turn about, he walking one day and his man the next. He came to the city in a patched mantle, walking, and entered by the gate; and the patriarch saw him in his rags, and said, sighing, that this was the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel the prophet.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 10; not verbatim.

passages.text: Umar granted the terms: the churches were safe and their clergy free; the people paid the tribute of the protected. He walked through the city with the patriarch, and prayed in the sanctuary of the Temple Mount where the Rock of David stood, cleared of the refuse that the Christians had heaped there; and he prayed at the south of the sanctuary, that the Muslims might not take the place of the Christians' worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 10; not verbatim.

title.en: Amr and the Books of Alexandria
title.zh: 阿慕爾與亞歷山大的藏書

region.zh: 埃及亞歷山大（實際定位）

texts.period: Event dated 642 CE in the story; English: S. Ockley, History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); Muir, The Caliphate (1891)

source.work: Simon Ockley, The History of the Saracens (Bohn ed. 1890); William Muir, The Caliphate (1891) — with the historian's note that the tale is contested

texts.license: Public domain (English editions 1890-91; Arabic original 13th century)

summary.en: The story told by Ibn al-Qifti and repeated by Ockley: after the capture of Alexandria, John the Grammarian asks the caliph for the books of the library. Umar answers: if they agree with the Qur'an they are superfluous; if against it, they are pernicious; burn them. The books are used to heat the city baths for six months. Modern historians find the story in no early source and doubt it; the tale belongs to the lore of the conquests.
summary.zh: 伊本·基夫提所傳、奧克萊重述的故事：攻克亞歷山大後，文法家約翰向哈里發求藏書。歐瑪爾答：若與古蘭經相合則為多餘；若相悖則為有害；燒之。其書供城中浴場燒水六個月。現代史家未於早期史料中見此說而存疑；此乃征服傳說之軼事。

sensitivity.note: A famous legend of contested historicity, recorded in Ockley's eighteenth-century English with the caution repeated here; presented as story, not as established event.

passages.text: When Amr had taken Alexandria, John the Grammarian asked of the caliph the books of the library of the city, that they might not be given to the soldiers. Umar answered: 'If the books agree with the Book of God, they are superfluous; if they contradict it, they are pernicious; burn them.' And the books were distributed to the baths of the city, and burned in them for six months.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the story as told in Ibn al-Qifti and repeated in Ockley, History of the Saracens (1890); not verbatim.

passages.text: The story is found in no early historian of the conquest; Muir records it with the caution that it is late and probably invented, and the modern reader should take it as a legend of the lore of the conquests — a tale about what it meant to burn a library, told long after the burning was forgotten or never happened.
passages.note: Historiographical note paraphrased from Muir, The Caliphate (1891); not verbatim.

title.en: The Battle of the Camel: Aisha's Litter
title.zh: 駱駝之戰：阿伊莎的駝轎

region.zh: 伊拉克巴士拉（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 656 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Aisha, the widow of the Prophet, rides from Mecca to Basra to avenge Uthman; Talha and Zubayr are with her. Ali comes up from Kufa. In the battle the camel of Aisha carries her litter into the field, and the fighting gathers around it; Talha and Zubayr fall. Ali wins, and sends the Prophet's widow home with honour — but the companions' first war against companions has been fought.
summary.zh: 先知遺孀阿伊莎自麥加赴巴士拉，欲為奧斯曼復仇；塔拉哈與祖拜爾同行。阿里自庫法來。戰中阿伊莎之駝載其轎入陣，廝殺聚於其周；塔拉哈與祖拜爾皆歿。阿里勝，以榮遣先知之遺孀返歸——然聖門弟子間首度兵戎相見。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the first civil war is read differently in Sunni and Shi'i memory; presented as received narrative.

passages.text: Uthman was slain in Medina, and Aisha, the widow of the Prophet, rode out to Basra to call his slayers to account, with Talha and Zubayr, two of the ten promised Paradise. Ali came up from Kufa to meet them; the parleys failed, and the two armies joined in battle under the walls of Basra.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19; not verbatim.

passages.text: Aisha sat in a litter on her camel, and the fighting gathered around her as around a standard; the battle was called the Battle of the Camel. Talha fell; Zubayr left the field, and was slain in a ravine by a man who came only for the spoils. At last the camel was hamstrung, and the litter sank; Ali won the day, and sent the Prophet's widow home to Medina with every honour — but the companions had fought companions, and the wound did not close.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 19; not verbatim.

region.zh: 幼發拉底河畔的綏芬（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 657 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Ali marches against Mu'awiya, governor of Syria. For days the armies fight; Amr ibn al-As, Mu'awiya's adviser, orders the soldiers to raise copies of the Qur'an on their spear-points and cry 'Let the Book of God decide.' The fight stops; Ali sees the trick — 'I knew them, O people; by night the pages were raised in sight of the Qur'an' — but his army compels him to arbitration. The arbitrators confer; the tide turns against Ali, and the Kharijites break away crying 'Judgment is God's alone.'
summary.zh: 阿里進軍敘利亞總督穆阿維亞。數日大戰；穆阿維亞謀士阿慕爾·本·阿斯令士兵將古蘭經抄本繫於矛端，高呼『讓主之經典裁決』。戰止；阿里識破詭計——『人們啊，我深知他們；夜間他們舉起書頁，卻不見古蘭經』——然其軍迫其行仲裁。仲裁者相商；局勢轉而不利於阿里，哈瓦利吉派高呼『惟主之裁決』而脫離。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; presented as received narrative.

passages.text: Ali marched against Mu'awiya, who had withheld his homage from Medina, and the armies met on the plain of Siffin by the Euphrates. For days the lines fought in relays; the spears and swords had decided nothing but the hour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Amr ibn al-As gave counsel to Mu'awiya: let the soldiers lift copies of the Qur'an on the points of their spears, crying, 'Let the Book of God judge between us.' And it was done; the battle stopped of itself. Ali said: 'I knew them — I tell you that these are the men of deception; by night they lifted pages that have nothing of the Qur'an in them.' But his army would not fight on, and compelled him to arbitration. The two arbitrators conferred at Adhruh; and the tide turned against Ali — and the strictest of his own soldiers broke away, crying, 'Judgment is God's alone; there is no arbitration between men.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 20; not verbatim.

region.zh: 麥地那奧斯曼宅（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 656 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: The besiegers close on the house of Uthman; Ali sends his sons to guard the door. The rebels break in at last, and the old caliph is struck as he recites the Book; his blood runs on the verses — 'and God will suffice thee against them that mock' — read on to the end. Medina has seen its first civil blood; the copy of the Qur'an that he was reading is said to be the one his own commission produced.
summary.zh: 圍困者逼至奧斯曼宅；阿里遣其子守門。叛者終破門而入；年邁哈里發誦經時被擊；其血流於經文之上——『主必使你免受嘲笑者之害』——經誦讀至終。麥地那首見同室操戈之血；相傳其誦讀的抄本，正是他主持委員會所定。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; the first caliph slain by Muslims is treated with restraint in all traditions.

passages.text: The malcontents gathered in Egypt and Kufa marched to Medina and besieged the house of Uthman. Ali sent his sons to keep the door, and blood was shed before it. The rebels broke in at last; and the old caliph, seated with the Book before him, was struck, and his blood ran over the page where he had read: 'They will say, art thou the one whom God and His Messenger blessed? — and God will suffice thee against the mockers.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17; not verbatim.

passages.text: It was the copy of the Qur'an which his own commission had gathered that lay before him, and the tale is told that he read to the end of the verse. His body was buried at night by his kin; Ali washed his hands, saying, 'God knows that I was innocent of his blood.' The Caliphate of Medina had seen its first civil blood, and the wound of the community was opened.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 17; not verbatim.

title.en: The Martyrdom of Ali in the Mosque of Kufa

region.zh: 庫法阿里清真寺（實際定位）

texts.period: Event 661 CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: A Kharijite, Ibn Muljam, waits for Ali at the dawn prayer of Ramadan in the mosque of Kufa. As the caliph is drawn from his couch of sleep and stands at prayer, the poisoned sword falls on the crown of his head. 'By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded'; the wound is mortal, and the words that follow are of the prayer, the fear of God, and the young man's death. Hasan buries him; the traditions read the murder as the price of arbitration.
summary.zh: 哈瓦利吉派刺客伊本·穆勒加姆於萊麥丹晨禮時候在庫法清真寺等候阿里。哈里發自睡榻起身立於禮拜時，淬毒之劍落於其頭頂。『以天房之主起誓，我已成功。』傷勢致命；臨終之言關乎禮拜、敬畏主、與青年刺客之死。哈桑葬之；諸傳統視此刺殺為仲裁之代價。

sensitivity.note: Early Islamic historiography; Ali's martyrdom is a cardinal event of Shi'i devotion; presented as received narrative without sectarian framing.

passages.text: Ibn Muljam, a Kharijite of the breakaway sect, had bound himself to kill Ali, and waited for him in the mosque of Kufa at the dawn prayer of Ramadan. As Ali came out of his couch of sleep and stood at prayer, the man struck him on the crown of the head with a sword dipped in poison.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ali cried, 'By the Lord of the Kaaba, I have succeeded.' The wound was mortal. He called his son Hasan, and spoke of the prayer, and of the fear of God, and of the young man who had killed him — 'Kill him gently, if I die of the wound, and do not mutilate him; I heard the Prophet say, do not mutilate even the dog.' And the First of the Muslims to be slain at prayer was buried in Kufa, and the caliphate passed out of the line of the companions.
passages.note: Paraphrase of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 21; not verbatim.

title.en: Mu'awiya: 'I Use Cunning Where Thou Usest Chivalry'
title.zh: 穆阿維亞：「你用騎士之勇，我用權謀」

region.zh: 大馬士革穆阿維亞宮廷（實際定位）

texts.period: Events 650s-660s CE; English: W. Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22
texts.license: Public domain (English edition 1891; Arabic originals 9th-10th centuries)

summary.en: Mu'awiya, first of the Umayyads, rules twenty years from Damascus with the tools of the scribe and the soldier. To the last of the companions who reproach him he answers with the famous word: 'By God, I do not use against thee the sword, or the whip, or the market, or the crowding of men; I use cunning where thou usest chivalry.' The anecdote lore of the court gathers around him — the Kharijite who threw his sandal, the man who called out in the mosque, and the letter that ended: 'Do not write to me of women; write to me of power.'
summary.zh: 伍麥葉王朝首主穆阿維亞自大馬士革以文書與士兵之術執政二十年。對最後一位責難他的聖門弟子，他答以名言：『我不用劍，不用鞭，不用市場，不用人潮相逼；你用騎士之勇，我用權謀。』宮廷軼事圍繞他累積——投擲其靴之哈瓦利吉派者、清真寺中高呼者、以及結尾寫道：『勿與我言婦人；與我言權力』的書信。

sensitivity.note: Anecdote lore of the Umayyad court as gathered in Muir from the Arabic historians; Mu'awiya is judged differently in Sunni and Shi'i memory.

passages.text: Mu'awiya ruled from Damascus for twenty years, the first of the Umayyads. To the men of the Prophet's generation who reproached him for his rule by scribes and soldiers, he gave the famous answer: 'By God, I do not use against thee the sword, or the whip, or the market, or the crowding of men; I use cunning where thou usest chivalry.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote lore of al-Tabari via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22; not verbatim.

passages.text: The court anecdotes gather round him: the Kharijite who flung his sandal at him in the mosque and was told that he would be given his blood-money if he could find his equal; the man who cried out against him and was made to drink honey as a punishment; and the letter to a man who sought a wife: 'Do not write to me of women; write to me of power.' And he was said to be the most patient and the most clement of the caliphs, and the least of them to be provoked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the anecdote lore via Muir, The Caliphate (1891), ch. 22; not verbatim.
